source_read: PDF, in-press proof pp. 1-19 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2013_NeurotoxicityFunctionalDeficits.pdf): all pages read as text with the proof line numbers, p. 5 rendered at 110 dpi to check paragraph breaks, Tables 1-4 and the reference list checked. Statements about Halpern et al. (2011) checked against PMC3053129 (Tables 1-4, Discussion) and about Schilt et al. (2007) against its PDF (pp. 728-732). Step 1 (blind extraction) was not part of this round.

design.note: Narrative review is right: no search, no eligibility criteria, no quantitative synthesis, and the review states its conclusion as a hypothesis chosen in advance (§1.2). The design_detail's description of the proof (pp. 1-19, printed article pp. 1466-1484) matches the file.

instrument.note: none-applicable with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as METHODS §5.3 requires for a narrative review; scripts/rob_vocab.py maps narrative-review to none-applicable.

key_findings.note: p. 2, proof lines 97-115: 'the empirical research literature is still fairly limited', neurocognition the only area extensively studied, and the core hypothesis as quoted.

49 vs 50, -19% to -46%, -21%, years and maximum dose, hair analysis, other drugs/sex/gene polymorphism/chronic tolerance monitored, subcortical reductions in heavier-use studies: all at p. 4, proof lines 186-210. The card does not repeat the occipital 46% figure here, which is correct: that figure is on p. 8 (§3.6), not in this paragraph (see my anchor note on task n=54).

Bauernfeind et al. (2011) at proof lines 256-263 and de Win et al. (2008) at 276-294, both on p. 5. The note that de Win and Schilt report the same 188-person cohort is right (Schilt et al., PDF pp. 728-729).
p. 5, proof lines 332-336, inside the first paragraph of §3.2.
I recomputed the fall from 17.4 to 9.2: 47.1%, so the card's 47% against the review's 'over 50%' is right.
p. 7, proof lines 500-505: 6.5 s, 8.9 s, 9.8 s, 15.3 s as printed.
The first part is at proof lines 560-565 (the paragraph runs 554-569) and the Rogers summary at 587-605; both on p. 7.

p. 9, proof lines 793-814: 2462 young people aged 14-24 reassessed after four years, 6.6% ecstasy and 2.3% amphetamines, disorders mostly preceding use; 1580 Dutch; 2143 Australian with odds ratio 1.0.
p. 12, proof lines 1158-1169, the 4th paragraph of §4.2.
p. 15, proof lines 1499-1521, including the sentence that it is difficult to think of any occupational activity that would not be impaired; no occupational study is cited anywhere in the section.

reporting_issues.note: Table 4 (p. 8) heads the row 'fMRI studies showing lower SERT' with McCann et al. (2008) and Kish et al. (2010), and §4.1 (p. 11, proof lines 1023-1024) calls them fMRI studies; both titles in the reference list name positron emission tomography.

Checked in PMC3053129: Table 3 gives spatial span forward p=0.18 and digits backwards p=0.15 in the heavier subgroup; Table 2 gives p=0.04 and p=0.05 in the whole group, and Table 3 spatial span forward p=0.04 in the moderate subgroup. The 2011b reference is P. Halpern et al., a survey of emergency department admissions, as the card says.

All four parts hold: proof line 412 gives '18-36 months'; Schilt et al. p. 731 gives 11.1 (SD 6.2) against 19.1 (SD 7.5) months, t=6.30, p<.001; the abstract (p. 728) says performance stayed within the normal range; Schilt et al. pp. 728-729 identify the 188-person Netherlands XTC Toxicity sample, mean age 22 years, aged 18-35, which the review calls teenagers.
47.1% by my calculation; the review says 'over 50%' at proof line 399 and '50% lower than their own baseline' at proof lines 1491-1492 (p. 15).

p. 11, proof lines 1026-1039: 'inversely associated with SERT binding levels' and, twelve lines later, 'a positive association between neurocognitive deficits, and serotonergic reductions'; Table 4 (p. 8) states the direction as lower SERT with poorer memory.
p. 13, proof lines 1250-1256. 136/329 = 41.3% by my calculation.
Q1 (p. 1), Q2 (p. 2), Q3 and the uncited-reference list (p. 15, proof lines 1540-1542: Darvesh and Gudelsky 2005, McDowell and Kleber 1994, Parrott 2012b).

domains.note: My own count of the reference list gives about 27 entries with Parrott among the authors, so 'roughly 30' is a fair approximation and is labelled as one.

I confirmed that Lyvers and Hasking (2004), Lyvers (2011), Gouzoulis-Mayfrank and Daumann (2006) and the Krebs and Johansen correspondence are absent from the reference list; Gouzoulis-Mayfrank and Daumann (2009) is cited, but for polydrug control rather than as a critique.

overall.note: High on the editors' checklist, and not less severe than the worst domain.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. The abstract's settled tone against §6.2's concession at p. 15 that endurance 'cannot be answered on current evidence' is the clearest instance, and the occupational passage has no supporting study.

missed: The prospective cohort cited at p. 6 (proof line 401) as 'Wagner et al. (2013)' has no entry in the proof's reference list: the only Wagner occurrences are co-authorships (Bosch et al., 2013; Mithoefer et al., 2011; Quednow et al., 2004). One of the two prospective cohorts the review relies on, and the 'second cohort' mentioned in cl_mdma_prospective, therefore cannot be identified from this source. This belongs in the reporting issues.

Nothing in the card covers §5.2 (p. 13, proof lines 1267-1309), where the review reports that people typically stop using on their own, that 90% of 430 people surveyed reported declining effects with repeated use (Verheyden et al., 2003a), and the author's hypothesis that serotonin loss drives chronic tolerance and escalation. METHODS §8 (v0.2.6) makes tolerance a standard question on every monograph, so this passage should be carded even though it is second-hand.

§3.10 (pp. 10-11, proof lines 930-954) summarizes the DAISY prenatal cohort (28 women who used a group mean of 25 tablets; lower Bayley psychomotor scores at 4 and 12 months with a dose relation; a report of more congenital abnormalities) and the abstract names developmental problems in children. Nothing in the card records it, and the monograph's special-populations section will need it with its second-hand status attached.

The review's argument that the SERT changes are due to MDMA rather than other drugs (p. 4, proof lines 211-217) rests partly on the theoretical claim that most other recreational drugs lack strong serotonergic effects. cl_mdma_sert_binding leans on this review, so the argument's basis should be on the card.

The 'Rogers et al. (2009)' the review uses for most of its memory figures is a Health Technology Assessment systematic review (HTA 13(6):1-315); the card could name it as such so that the editor cites the synthesis rather than this review's description of it.
